setup.zh: 傍晚，山门外：舅舅在等你，镖师葛六也在。「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱。给不给，你自己掂量。」
setup.en: Dusk outside the gate: your uncle is waiting, and so is the escort Ge Liu. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money. Pay or don't — weigh it yourself."

recap.zh: 开山门那天傍晚：舅舅在山门外等你，没让马三把你劝退；葛六说破了林子里那颗石子，又说「有人的地方，就有公中」。
recap.en: The evening the gate opened: your uncle waited outside the gate and wouldn't let Ma San talk you into leaving; Ge Liu told you who paid for the pebble in the forest, and that "wherever there are people, there's a common fund".

en: Outside the gate, your uncle looks up.
"Wherever there are people, there's a common fund."

story.zh:
那天傍晚，新入门的弟子许出山门，跟送考的家里人说一句话，一炷香为限。执事把那面兵器架子抬上来了，小满取回了爷爷那张弓——第三排左数第七个，一个手指头也没人碰过——背在背上，跑出山门。

山门外的石坪边上，坐着葛六，短刀横在膝盖上，腰里的钱袋瘪着。他看见小满，招了招手，道：「杂灵根，进了？」小满道：「进了。」葛六道：「林子里那颗石子，是马三一锭银子买的。我没接，他扣了我五两。」他站起身，把短刀插回腰里，「进了门，头一件事，有人找你收钱——一个月三块灵石，先得交出去一块。有人的地方，就有公中。给不给，你自己掂量；你这样的，掂量得清。」说完，他顺着石阶下山去了。小满站在那里，把这两句话在心里各记了一笔。

石坪那头，有人叫他：「满子。」是老周，阿禾她爹，裤腿上全是泥，在山门外头站了一整天，脸都晒脱了皮。他搓着手，想问又不敢问，憋了半天，道：「我家禾……」小满道：「进了。真灵根，中上。」老周愣了一愣，蹲下去，拿两只手捂着脸，捂了好一会儿，才站起来，从怀里摸出一个鸡蛋，塞进小满手里：「她欠你的。先还一个。」话音没落，山门里闪出一个人来，红鼻头，两根小辫子，一把把那个鸡蛋从小满手里拿了回去，看也不看他，只对她爹道：「我家的账，我自己还。」她把鸡蛋揣进怀里，转身进了山门。老周冲小满尴尬地笑了一笑。小满低头看看自己空了的手，心想：这下好，三个半，一个也没少。

舅舅站在第三百级石阶边上，也不知站了多久，青布长衫的下摆全是泥。他一看见小满，先不问考上没考上，先问：「饿不饿？」小满道：「饿。」舅舅从怀里摸出一个炊饼——早上在山脚下买的，他自己没舍得吃——塞进他手里，这才问：「……考上了？」小满道：「外门。」

舅舅一把抓住了他的胳膊，抓得死紧。他转过身，对着旁边一个不认识的老头，大声道：「我外甥！考上了！三百级，一口气！」那老头吓了一跳。舅舅又对着另一个不认识的妇人道：「我外甥！」那妇人也吓了一跳。

马三从人堆里挤了过来，没理小满，把舅舅拉到一边，压低了嗓子，脸上堆着笑：「沈家舅舅，商量个事。杂灵根，下下之资，在山上熬也是白熬。你让他自己退了，今年的山风钱，免一年。」舅舅这一辈子，见了马三从来不抬头。这一回，他抬起了头：「不退。家里有孩子进了仙门的，马家不敢收租——这话，满县城都知道。」马三的笑一下子没了。他盯着舅舅看了好一会儿，转身走到马小宝的滑竿跟前，把一包桂花糕塞给儿子，低声道：「在山上给我看着他。他待不住，沈家的租，就还是咱家的。」说罢，带着家丁下山去了。

舅舅望着他的背影，腰杆挺了一挺，又道：「当年，我也爬到了一百八十级——」小满道：「舅舅。」舅舅道：「……一百六十级。」

小满道：「舅舅，一百六十级那里，崖壁上刻满了字，都是在那一级上坐下过的人刻的。」舅舅不说话了。他把脸转过去，朝着泗水那边，看了很久。小满道：「舅舅，我替你走上来了。」舅舅没有回头。过了好一会儿，他才开口，声音有点哑，道：「……风大。」他拿袖子在脸上抹了一把，又抹了一把，然后转回来，把小满背上那张弓扶正了，把他的衣领翻好——翻衣领的那一下，同他姐姐一模一样——道：「回去吧。一炷香到了。」

小满走进山门，回头看，舅舅还站在那儿。门口的石坪边上，牛棚里那对兖州父子也在：儿子在一百四十级上坐下了，没进得来，这时候蜷在石阶边，脸朝着崖壁；他爹坐在旁边，一锅一锅地抽旱烟。山门合上以后，舅舅挪过去，挨着那个爹坐下了。他没提自己的外甥，只道：「我当年，也没上去。爬到一百六十级，腿就动不了了。下了山，去县里学打算盘，如今在济世堂做账房，娶了媳妇，生了个闺女。」他顿了一顿，又道：「挺好的。」那孩子的肩膀动了一下。兖州那个爹问他：「老哥，你当年，到底爬到了多少级？」舅舅想了一想，道：「一百六十级。」那是他这辈子，头一回，没有多说十级。

天擦黑的时候，舅舅下山。走到石阶头上，那个光脚的孩子还蹲在山门边，考牌攥在手里，脚底板上的草叶子磨烂了，渗着血丝。舅舅从他身边走过去，走了三级，又走回来，在他跟前蹲下，道：「家在哪？」「兖州，汶上。」「家里知道你来？」那孩子不吭声，过了一会儿，道：「二亩坡地，押给里正了，换的路费。说好了，考上了，五两银子赎回来。」舅舅没说话。他想起自己在一百六十级上坐的那一炷香，想起下了山那年，县城里没一个人问他一句往后怎么办。他把包袱里最后一块干粮掏出来，塞给那孩子，道：「会数数么？」「会。数到一千。」「济世堂缺一个抓药跑腿的，管吃管住，一个月三百文。地，一年赎得回来。」他顿了一顿，「三年以后，你要还想来，我放你三天假。」那孩子攥着那块干粮，看了他半天，道：「……你是谁？」舅舅站起身来，拍了拍膝盖上的土，道：「一个爬到一百六十级的。」

两个人一前一后下了石阶。走到山脚，天已经黑透了。马家包下的那家客栈门口，灯笼底下围着一圈人，当中跪着一个，是葛六。马三坐在门槛上剔牙，镖局的掌柜站在他旁边，把一块红绸从葛六的刀鞘上一圈一圈解下来，道：「马三爷是县里头一号的主顾。往后，县城镖局，没你这一号人。」两个家丁一左一右，把葛六的短刀折成了两截，扔在泥里。葛六一声不吭，等他们折完了，自己站起来，捡起那半截刀，插回鞘里。他从舅舅身边走过去，认出了他，咧嘴一笑，嘴角有血：「老哥，二十年了，今天我也在台阶上坐下了一回。」舅舅道：「往后呢？」葛六往北边黑地里看了一眼：「往后？马家的镖，有人走；马家不想让人走的路，也得有人走。」说完，他走进黑地里去了。马三在门槛上吐了一口唾沫，朝山上那一片灯火看了很久，招手叫过一个家丁：「牵马，连夜回蒙山，告诉老爷——沈家的租，收不得了。可后山是马家的山，山上的风也姓马。从明儿起，沈老大进山，打一只兔子，交一只兔子。」那家丁应声去了。舅舅站在灯笼照不着的地方，一字一字听得清清楚楚。他把那孩子往身后拉了拉，没往县城那条路上走。他转过身，朝着蒙山的方向，走进了夜里。
story.en:
Toward evening that day the new disciples were allowed out of the gate to say a word to the family who'd brought them, for the length of one stick of incense. The stewards had carried the weapons rack up; Xiaoman took his grandfather's bow back — third row, seventh from the left, not a finger laid on it — slung it on his back, and ran out of the gate.

At the edge of the terrace outside the gate sat Ge Liu, his short knife across his knees, his purse flat at his waist. He saw Xiaoman and beckoned. "Mixed root. In?" Xiaoman said, "In." Ge Liu said: "That pebble in the forest — Ma San bought it with a silver ingot. I didn't take it, so he docked me five taels." He stood and slid the knife back into his belt. "Once you're through the gate, first thing, someone comes to collect money — three spirit stones a month, and one has to go straight back out. Wherever there are people, there's a common fund. Pay or don't — weigh it yourself; your sort can weigh it." And with that he went off down the stair. Xiaoman stood there and put each of the two sentences down on his books.

Across the terrace someone called him: "Man'zi." It was old Zhou, Ahe's father, mud to the knees, who had stood outside the gate all day till the skin peeled off his sunburnt face. He rubbed his hands, wanting to ask and not daring, and at last got out: "My He…" Xiaoman said, "She's in. A true root, just above the middle." Old Zhou stared, squatted down, covered his face with both hands a good while, then stood up, took an egg from his coat and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand. "She owes you. Here's one back." Before he'd finished, someone darted out of the gate — red nose, two little braids — took the egg back out of Xiaoman's hand without so much as a look at him, and said only to her father: "My family's debts, I pay myself." She tucked the egg into her jacket and went back through the gate. Old Zhou gave Xiaoman an awkward smile. Xiaoman looked down at his empty hand and thought: well, three and a half, and not one less.

His uncle stood at the edge of the three hundredth step; how long he'd been standing there no one knew, the hem of his blue cotton gown all mud. The moment he saw Xiaoman, before asking whether he'd passed, he asked: "Hungry?" Xiaoman said, "Hungry." His uncle took a griddle cake from his coat — bought at the foot of the mountain that morning, and he hadn't had the heart to eat it himself — pressed it into his hand, and only then asked: "…Got in?" Xiaoman said, "Outer court."

His uncle seized his arm and gripped it tight. He turned to an old man he didn't know and said loudly: "My nephew! Got in! Three hundred steps, one go!" The old man jumped. His uncle turned to a woman he didn't know: "My nephew!" The woman jumped too.

Ma San pushed out of the crowd, ignored Xiaoman, drew the uncle aside, and said low, all smiles: "Brother Shen, a word. A mixed root, lowest of the low — it's wasted effort sticking it out up here. Have him withdraw of his own accord, and this year's mountain-wind money is waived." All his life the uncle had never looked up at Ma San. This time he looked up. "He won't withdraw. A family with a child inside the immortal gate — the Mas daren't take rent from it; the whole county knows that." Ma San's smile vanished. He stared at the uncle a good while, then went to Ma Xiaobao's chair, thrust a packet of osmanthus cakes at his son, and said low: "Keep an eye on him up here. If he can't stick it out, the Shens' rent is ours again." And off he went down the mountain with his servants.

His uncle watched his back and straightened a little, and said again: "Back then, I climbed to step one hundred and eighty myself —" Xiaoman said, "Uncle." His uncle said: "…One hundred and sixty."

Xiaoman said, "Uncle, at step one hundred and sixty the cliff wall is covered in writing — all carved by people who sat down on that step." His uncle fell silent. He turned his face toward the Si and looked a long time. Xiaoman said, "Uncle, I walked up for you." His uncle didn't turn round. After a good while he spoke, his voice a little hoarse: "…Windy." He wiped his face with his sleeve, and wiped it again; then turned back, set the bow straight on Xiaoman's back, turned his collar straight — that turn of the collar exactly like his sister's — and said: "Go on back. The incense is out."

Xiaoman walked through the gate and looked back; his uncle was still standing there. On the terrace by the gate the father and son from Yanzhou were there too: the son had sat down at step one hundred and forty and never got in; now he lay curled by the stair, face to the cliff, and his father sat beside him smoking a long pipe, bowl after bowl. When the gate had closed, the uncle moved over and sat down beside that father. He didn't mention his nephew; he said only: "I didn't get up either, back then. Got to step one hundred and sixty, and my legs wouldn't move. Came down, went to the county to learn the abacus; now I keep the books at the Jishi Hall, took a wife, had a daughter." He paused. "It's all right." The boy's shoulders moved. The Yanzhou father asked him: "Old brother, how many steps did you really climb, back then?" The uncle thought a moment. "One hundred and sixty." It was the first time in his life he hadn't added ten.

At nightfall the uncle went down. At the head of the stair the barefoot boy was still squatting by the gate, the tag in his hand, the grass under his soles worn to shreds and seeping blood. The uncle walked past him, went three steps down, came back, and squatted in front of him. "Where's home?" "Yanzhou. Wenshang." "Does your family know you came?" The boy said nothing; after a while: "Two mu of hillside, pledged to the headman for the road money. The deal was: get in, and the five taels buy it back." The uncle said nothing. He thought of the stick of incense he'd sat through on step one hundred and sixty, and of the year he came down, when not one soul in the county town asked him what he'd do now. He took the last of the food from his bundle and pressed it on the boy. "Can you count?" "Yes. To a thousand." "The Jishi Hall needs a boy to fetch medicines. Board and bed, three hundred coppers a month. The land, you'll buy back in a year." He paused. "Three years from now, if you still want to come, I'll give you three days off." The boy gripped the food and looked at him a long time. "…Who are you?" The uncle stood, dusted the earth off his knees, and said: "One who climbed to a hundred and sixty."

The two of them went down the stair one behind the other. By the foot of the mountain it was full dark. At the door of the inn the Mas had taken, under the lanterns, a ring of people stood round a man on his knees: Ge Liu. Ma San sat on the threshold picking his teeth, and the master of the escort bureau stood beside him, unwinding the red silk from Ge Liu's sheath turn by turn. "Third Master Ma is the county's biggest customer. From now on, the county escort bureau has no such man as you." Two servants, one either side, snapped Ge Liu's short knife in two and threw it in the mud. Ge Liu said not a word; when they had done, he got up by himself, picked up the half of the knife, and slid it back into the sheath. Passing the uncle, he knew him and grinned, blood at the corner of his mouth. "Old brother — twenty years on, today I sat down on a step for once too." The uncle said, "And after this?" Ge Liu looked off into the dark to the north. "After this? Somebody walks the Mas' caravans; somebody has to walk the roads the Mas don't want walked, too." And he walked off into the dark. Ma San spat from the threshold and looked a long time at the lights up the mountain, then beckoned a servant. "Saddle a horse, ride back to Mount Meng tonight, tell the master: the Shens' rent can't be collected. But the back mountain is the Mas' mountain, and the wind on it's surnamed Ma too. From tomorrow, when old Shen goes up the mountain, one rabbit shot, one rabbit handed over." The servant went. The uncle stood where the lanterns didn't reach and heard it word for word. He pulled the boy behind him, and didn't take the road to the county town. He turned toward Mount Meng and walked off into the night.

exits.means: pays the one stone to the common fund, keeps the peace for now

refuse.en: You have no spirit stones on you.

what.zh: 外门的「公中」：收了你一块灵石。
what.en: The outer court's "common fund": took one of your spirit stones.

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路。他掂量出来的是：一块灵石，买一个「懂事」，买马小宝一个月不来找麻烦。这笔账，眼下划得来。

第二天一早，饭堂门口，他从怀里摸出一块灵石，交了。马小宝掂了一掂，冲他笑，笑得跟他爹一模一样。

他心里却记了一笔：公中，一块。马小宝。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair. What he weighed out was: one spirit stone buys "knowing his place", buys a month of Ma Xiaobao leaving him alone. For now, the sum comes out in his favour.

Next morning at the refectory door he took a spirit stone from his jacket and handed it over. Ma Xiaobao weighed it in his palm and grinned at him, a grin exactly like his father's.

But in his heart he entered a line: Common fund, one stone. Ma Xiaobao.

exits.means: refuses to pay the common fund

story.zh:
小满把葛六那两句话，在心里掂量了一路，掂量出来一个字：不。他把怀里的灵石一块一块放进他娘给的那个空钱袋里，叮，叮，叮。空钱袋里，头一回有了东西。

他知道往后会怎样：马小宝不会当着人的面动手，他会等。他爹就是这么收租的——先笑，再等，等你以为没事了，门就飞了。那就等。
story.en:
Xiaoman weighed Ge Liu's two sentences all the way up the stair, and weighed out one word: no. He put the spirit stones from his jacket one by one into the empty purse his mother had given him — *ting, ting, ting*. For the first time, the empty purse held something.

He knew what would come of it: Ma Xiaobao wouldn't lift a hand in front of people; he'd wait. That was how his father collected rent — grin first, then wait, wait till you think it's over, and then the door flies. Then let him wait.
